text: Again there came a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.
The LORD said to Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD, "From roaming the earth and walking back and forth across it."

The LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds fast to his integrity, though you incited me against him to ruin him without cause."
Satan answered the LORD, "Skin for skin! A man will give up all he has to save his own life.
But just stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse you to your face.

versions.text: But stretch out your hand and strike his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse you to your face."
versions.explanation: The verb נגע means "touch," the same verb used in 1:11; "strike" overstates it and loses the deliberate echo of Satan's earlier challenge. A footnote could note that the Hebrew literally reads "bless," used here as a euphemism for cursing.

versions.text: But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse you to your face."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew particle נָא adds a note of urging ("just" / "do go ahead") to Satan's challenge, which the present rendering leaves out. Adding "just" restores the nuance without lengthening the line, and it reads well aloud. The current rendering is otherwise accurate. It would also help the reader to note that the Hebrew literally reads "bless" here, a euphemism for cursing.

text: The LORD said to Satan, "Very well, he is in your hands, but spare his life."
So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
And Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself while he sat among the ashes.
His wife said to him, "Are you still holding on to your integrity? Curse God and die!"
He answered her, "You are talking like a foolish woman. Shall we accept good from God and not accept trouble?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

versions.text: He answered her, "You are talking like a foolish woman. Shall we accept good from God and not accept evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.
versions.explanation: הָרָע here denotes calamity or adversity rather than moral evil; rendering it "evil" can suggest God is the source of moral wickedness. "Trouble" (as used for the same idea in v. 11) avoids that implication and keeps the rhythm.

text: When Job's three friends heard of all the trouble that had come upon him, each of them set out from his own place—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They agreed to go together to show him sympathy and comfort him.
When they looked up from a distance, they could not recognize him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and tossed dust into the air over their heads.

versions.text: When they looked up from a distance, they could not recognize him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and threw dust on their heads toward the sky.
versions.explanation: "Threw dust on their heads toward the sky" is confusing when read aloud, since the dust cannot go both onto their heads and toward the sky; the Hebrew pictures dust thrown upward so that it falls on their heads.

text: Then they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw how great his suffering was.
